ai.definition: De novo protein design is a computational approach that involves designing and synthesizing entirely new protein structures from scratch, without relying on existing natural proteins as templates.
ai.howItWorks: The process begins by defining the desired function of the protein. Computational algorithms are then used to predict potential sequences and structures that could achieve this function. Once promising designs are identified, they are synthesized in the lab and tested for their ability to fold into the predicted structure and perform the intended function.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the limitations of traditional protein engineering methods, which often rely on modifying existing proteins rather than creating entirely new ones with novel functions.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves synthesizing the designed DNA sequences using techniques like PCR amplification followed by gene synthesis. These genes are then inserted into expression vectors and expressed in host cells such as bacteria or yeast to produce the protein.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes computational design, sequence optimization, protein synthesis, and functional testing. Computational tools play a crucial role in predicting structural stability and function before physical synthesis.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the complexity of the designed proteins, the efficiency of gene synthesis technologies, and the cost of expression systems used for protein production.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is promising as de novo protein design has the potential to revolutionize biotech applications but faces challenges in scaling up and regulatory approval.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are still developing, with varying requirements depending on the intended application of the designed proteins. Safety and efficacy must be rigorously tested before market entry.
ai.risks: Risks include technical challenges such as ensuring proper protein folding and function, intellectual property concerns, and potential regulatory hurdles.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain due to high initial research costs and the need for successful commercialization of specific applications. However, if successful, it could lead to significant market opportunities in pharmaceuticals, diagnostics, and materials science.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving computational tools, reducing production costs, and expanding the range of functions that can be achieved through de novo protein design.

glossary.def: From scratch or anew; not based on existing templates.
Modifying existing proteins to improve their properties or create new ones with specific functions.

subsystems.name: Computational design engine
subsystems.role: generates protein backbones and amino-acid sequences that fold into a desired shape.

subsystems.name: DNA synthesis and assembly
subsystems.role: turns the designed sequence into physical DNA.

subsystems.name: Expression system
subsystems.role: makes the protein from the DNA.

subsystems.name: Purification and analytics
subsystems.role: isolates the protein and checks its purity.

subsystems.name: Structural and functional testing
subsystems.role: verifies that the protein actually folds and works as intended.

buildSteps.title: Define the target function
buildSteps.detail: Decide what the protein must do — for example, bind a specific receptor, catalyse a reaction, or form a particular scaffold.

buildSteps.title: Generate a backbone
buildSteps.detail: Software proposes a three-dimensional protein fold that can present the required functional groups in the right geometry.

buildSteps.title: Design the sequence
buildSteps.detail: Amino acids are chosen so the chain will fold into that backbone and carry out the function, avoiding unwanted interactions.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise the gene
buildSteps.detail: The DNA sequence is assembled from short oligonucleotides or ordered from a commercial supplier.

buildSteps.title: Express the protein
buildSteps.detail: The gene is inserted into host cells, which are grown and induced to produce the protein.

buildSteps.title: Purify the protein
buildSteps.detail: Cells are broken open and the protein is separated from other material using chromatography.

buildSteps.title: Characterise the design
buildSteps.detail: Structure is solved by cryo-electron microscopy or X-ray crystallography, and function is tested with binding or activity assays.

buildSteps.title: Optimise and iterate
buildSteps.detail: If the protein is unstable or inactive, mutations are made and the cycle repeats until it meets the specification.

buildSteps.title: Scale up and formulate
buildSteps.detail: Successful designs are produced in larger quantities and prepared for their final use, such as a drug or an industrial catalyst.

prerequisites.why: knowing how sequence maps to shape is the foundation for designing a new fold.
tools can now propose plausible backbones, but reliability varies with the target function.
making a designed gene quickly and cheaply is essential for testing many variants.
cryo-electron microscopy and X-ray crystallography confirm that the design folded as intended.
without a reliable way to produce the protein, a design remains only a computer file.

pathway.milestone: designed proteins used as research reagents and as clinical candidates for vaccines and antivirals
pathway.unlocks: proof that de novo designs can function in living systems.

pathway.milestone: first approved medicines built on de novo designed proteins
pathway.unlocks: a new route to drugs that are hard to make by other means.

pathway.milestone: designed enzymes for industrial catalysis and environmental clean-up
pathway.unlocks: replacing some chemical processes with milder, more specific biocatalysis.

pathway.milestone: designed proteins as components of smart materials and molecular machines
pathway.unlocks: programmable matter at the nanoscale, from responsive gels to targeted delivery systems.
